# The communities, with more knowledge to save the bay of Cartagena

**This place, a source of national pride and a tourism treasure, is in critical condition. For the past seven years, research has been providing precise diagnoses that facilitate decision-making to mitigate the effects of pollution and improve the quality of life for the people in the surrounding area.**

- Communities, with more knowledge to save Cartagena Bay

There are places you visit and are left with the feeling of never wanting to return. For me, one of those was Cartagena de Indias in December 2019. Although I know there are inequalities everywhere, the ones I noticed there really shocked me.

I recently returned for work reasons and today I just think how much I would like to be able to return to do work with the communities, to return to learn more stories like that of Mirla Aaron Freite.

She is 51 years old. Her days begin very early. Together with “Popi,” her mother, she welcomes the neighbors with a hot cup of coffee around five in the morning. She is the ears and voice of her neighbors.

She's a community leader, and it doesn't take a genius to guess that more than just blood runs through her veins. Her eyes reflect that spark of hope for a brighter future: passion and optimism. Perhaps those two words could also define her life.

And there's no other way. It seems he always knows what to do and who to turn to in order to solve the problems that plague his community, a small island located south of the urban center of Cartagena, similar in size to the municipality of Itagüí in Antioquia.

Mirla lives there, this social leader originally from Santa Marta, who after going back and forth to other places on the Colombian Caribbean coast decided to settle 25 years ago in this territory where the sand of the sea blends with the earth of its unpaved streets.

She has two children: a young dreamer who migrated to Berlin (Germany) in 2018 and a trans girl who has learned from her mother to assert her rights.

Tierra Bomba is a place in the middle of the sea, but its nearly 3,500 inhabitants lack access to drinking water. There, job opportunities are almost nonexistent, yet tourism generates more than half of the gross domestic product (GDP) of the department of Bolívar right across the water.

On one side of the beach, children bathe amidst the boats of their parents and uncles, but about 10 or 15 meters away, diapers, masks, and many plastic bags float.

How to get to Tierra Bomba?

This is one of the questions suggested by Google, and the search results usually show a different reality than what I saw.

Neither is that a lie nor is what I'm telling you the absolute truth, but coins definitely have two sides and discovering a little of these dualities was, in itself, the objective of my trip.

Tierra Bomba is home to people from various parts of the country, especially from nearby departments.

It has also been a destination for many Venezuelan migrants. It is a town that lives primarily off tourism-related activities such as selling food and handicrafts, providing massage services, and traditional fishing.

Like everyone else, the pandemic hit them hard, both emotionally and financially. “We practically survived thanks to the fishermen. We waited for them every day. Between two and three small fish per family. They helped us a lot,” Mirla recalls about the most brutal days of the social upheaval caused by that almost invisible agent whose consequences we still feel today.

[![Image of a man on a boat, in the sea off Cartagena, conducting research](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/738c8ebc-6d2c-47d0-a25e-876fa3480625/web/FOTO-COMUNIDADES-CARTAGENA.jpg?crop=yes&k=c&w=944&h=540&itok=3vECqj7v)](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias/publicaciones/descubre-y-crea/edicion-177/las-comunidades-con-mas-conocimientos-para-salvar-la-bahia-de-cartagena)

![](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias/publicaciones/descubre-y-crea/edicion-177/las-comunidades-con-mas-conocimientos-para-salvar-la-bahia-de-cartagena)

The research is funded by the International Development Research Centre of Canada. It is led by EAFIT University, with participation from the University of the Andes and the University of Cartagena, and support from the Regional Autonomous Corporation of the Canal del Dique and the Hernán Echavarría Olózaga Foundation. **Photo: Pixabay**

But both before and after COVID-19, Tierra Bomba must face challenges of great magnitude that, due to their complexity, do not have a single solution.

This refers to the high pollution of the Cartagena bay, the common area of ​​Tierra Bomba and the communities of Barú, Ararca, Caño del Oro, Bocachica, Punta Arena and Pasacaballos that live around this body of water.

For nearly 500 years, this has been the main port of the Colombian Caribbean, also known as the "Gateway to Trade in the Americas." Thanks to its geographic location, it is a strategic point for the transport of goods and the establishment of hundreds of businesses.

Until just a few decades ago it was preserved as one of the most precious ecosystems in the country, but everything has changed: today the bay is a patient that requires intensive care and hopefully there were methods as effective as a vaccine to solve it.

> “I’ve been involved in high-level European projects, and this one is exactly at the same level, or even higher. The way the communities are involved here is fantastic. It’s something I’ve personally never seen before.” Flávio Martins, research associate on the project, University of Algarve (Portugal).

###### Impacts on politics and social empowerment

Based on the results of Basic, the Administrative Court of Bolívar ruled last year in a lawsuit against national and local institutions, ministries, the Mayor's Office of Cartagena and even the National Navy.

The creation of an urgent recovery plan was ordered, and the Inter-institutional Environmental Committee for the Management of Cartagena Bay was created for this purpose by the Ministry of Environment.

En esta instancia se cuenta con la participación de diversos actores de sectores y por primera vez en la historia se incluyen habitantes de la zona. Una importante herramienta para ello fue un diplomado dirigido a 20 representantes institucionales y 40 ciudadanos.

Entre ellas, Mirla, quien además es alta consultiva de nivel nacional, Mujer ONU y estudiante de último año de Derecho.

“Basic no te da un pescado, sino que te enseña a pescar. Ser una líder exige tener este tipo de capacidades y realmente no las teníamos. Hoy podemos incidir, defender, apoyar y aportar a nuestras problemáticas”.

[![Image of training attendees showing their certificates](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/3ad97c03-186a-482d-86a9-e504071233ee/web/FOTO-COMUNIDADES2.jpg?crop=yes&k=c&w=944&h=540&itok=WzJvUmBI)](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias/publicaciones/descubre-y-crea/edicion-177/las-comunidades-con-mas-conocimientos-para-salvar-la-bahia-de-cartagena)

![](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias/publicaciones/descubre-y-crea/edicion-177/las-comunidades-con-mas-conocimientos-para-salvar-la-bahia-de-cartagena)

Con las capacitaciones a la comunidad y a instituciones, los habitantes de la ciudad tienen mayores herramientas para asumir la defensa de su territorio. **Foto: Cortesía del proyecto.**

###### Un futuro prominente

Hasta final del año 2023, el proyecto contará con una tercera fase para el desarrollo de alertas tempranas que permitan hacer pronósticos de eventos de contaminación.

Con esto se podrá generar información y conocimiento para las autoridades ambientales. También se espera seguir buscando recursos para su sostenibilidad y un

mayor impacto en las personas.

Definitivamente, esta iniciativa es un referente para países en desarrollo que enfrentan realidades similares y es reconocer, como dice Mirla, que en el trabajo en equipo se logran soluciones comunes y acertadas, “que detrás de la ciencia hay grandes seres humanos, personas que han entendido que no existe un conocimiento técnico que pueda ser absoluto si no encuentra una línea directa de conexión con los saberes y los desafíos que tienen las comunidades”.

###### Virus contra bacterias, la propuesta para el sector porcino de PhageLife desde EAFIT

En una granja porcina, una infección bacteriana puede poner en riesgo la salud de los animales y la productividad del negocio. Además, el problema se vuelve más complejo cuando las bacterias dejan de responder a los antibióticos que antes permitían combatirlas. Para explorar otra vía, la empresa [PhageLife](https://phagelife.co/) desarrolla soluciones personalizadas con bacteriófagos, virus naturales capaces de eliminar bacterias específicas.
